title: Controllability as prior knowledge does not relax the conditions for data-driven stabilization
author: Amir Shakouri, Henk J. van Waarde, Tren M.J.T. Baltussen, W.P.M.H. Heemels
work: Data-Driven Stabilization Using Prior Knowledge on Stabilizability and Controllability
difficulty_reason: The counted statement is the article's Theorem 5 (source label 'th:1'): for a true system in Sigma_cont, Sigma_cont-informativity of the data for stabilization is equivalent to plain informativity for stabilization, and any gain that stabilizes every data-consistent controllable system stabilizes every data-consistent system. The unit is above ordinary PhD qualifying level because the counted proof is not a citation and cannot be reached by textbook linear algebra alone: the authors perturb the true system along the data-consistency directions through the set of (A_0,B_0) with A_0 X_- + B_0 U_- = 0, and the argument then rests on two auxiliary results whose complete proofs are retained inside the unit. The first, Lemma 7, shows that a controllable pair stays controllable along the whole affine line except for at most n^2 parameter values, by exhibiting a square submatrix of the Kalman controllability matrix that is nonsingular at the controllable point and whose determinant is a polynomial of degree at most n^2. The second, Lemma 9, shows that if a matrix pencil M + delta N is Schur on a half-line minus finitely many points then N is nilpotent and the pencil is Schur on the whole real line, by observing that the traces of all powers are bounded polynomials on that half-line, hence constant, and then invoking Horn and Johnson's characterization of equality of spectra through traces of powers. Combining data informativity with a polynomial perturbation argument and deducing a stability conclusion for one uncontrollable data-consistent system from a hypothesis on all controllable data-consistent systems, and thereby showing that controllability as prior knowledge does not relax the stabilization conditions, is research-level data-driven control theory rather than a qualifying-examination exercise.
